Anchorage breeding population — results summary

Published

4 November 2026

NoteHow to read this report

Abundance is estimated on a relative scale — the counts are a volunteer index, not a census. Read the shape of the trajectory and the growth rate \(\lambda\); the absolute number of birds is not identified and is not reported here.

Recruitment (psi1, psi2) is a composite probability: survive and return to breed locally. It is not juvenile survival, and should not be compared against published juvenile survival estimates.

1 Overview

This integrated population model combines three data sources into one likelihood so that each informs a shared set of demographic rates.

NoteThe counts cover the same ground as the demographic data — deliberately

The volunteer survey covers 32 wetlands across roughly 67 km of upper Cook Inlet, but every marked bird and every monitored nest comes from the Anchorage bowl (Figure 1). Fitting all 32 would make λ a statement about a wider population than the survival and productivity estimates meant to explain it, and the decomposition further down this report would be comparing the two. Since 2026-11-04 the count stream is restricted to the 27 wetlands in the bowl, dropping both Palmer Hay Flats accesses, Eklutna, Big Lake and Lynn Fuller’s Ponds — 37–67 km out, and 22.6% of all birds counted. They are not drawn in Figure 1.

The restriction makes the decline steeper, not weaker: λ 0.939 → 0.930, with P(λ < 1) = 0.997 either way. The wider-area fit is kept as a sensitivity. The list and reasoning are at the top of scripts/LEYE_IPM.R.

Recruitment carries a two-year lag: chicks are absent from the breeding site until they recruit, and chick data from both eras show recruitment split roughly evenly between ages 1 and 2. Recruits enter the breeding class directly, so there is no separate juvenile stage — volunteer counts cannot distinguish non-breeding age-1 birds from breeding adults. The full formulation follows.

2.3 Statistical formulation

Transcribed from scripts/LEYE_IPM.R. Indices: \(t\) = year (1…\(T\), 2014–2026), \(i\) = count record, \(j\) = marked individual, \(m\) = nest, \(w\) = survey week, \(k\) = wetland.

Process model. Two free initial years, because recruitment lags two years and there is nothing to build \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) from:

\[ \begin{aligned} N_1,\, N_2 &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ 50)\ \text{truncated at } 0 \\[2pt] R_t &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(N_{t-1}\,\frac{f_{t-1}}{2}\,\psi_1 \;+\; N_{t-2}\,\frac{f_{t-2}}{2}\,\psi_2\right) \\[2pt] S_t &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(N_{t-1}\,\phi_{t-1}\right) \\[2pt] I_t &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(N_{t-1}\,\omega\right) \\[2pt] N_t &= S_t + R_t + I_t \\[2pt] \lambda_t &= N_{t+1} \,/\, N_t \end{aligned} \qquad t = 3,\dots,T \]

Vital rates.

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{logit} \phi_t &= \mu_\phi + \varepsilon_{\phi,t}, &\varepsilon_{\phi,t} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_\phi) &&\text{adult survival} \\[2pt] \operatorname{logit} s_t &= \mu_s + \varepsilon_{s,t}, &\varepsilon_{s,t} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_s) &&\text{nest success} \\[2pt] f_t &= s_t \cdot C \cdot q &&&&\text{fledglings per pair} \\[2pt] \psi_1 &= \pi\,\kappa &&&&\text{recruit at age 1} \\[2pt] \psi_2 &= \pi\,(1-\kappa) &&&&\text{recruit at age 2} \end{aligned} \]

with \(C = 4\) (modal clutch) and \(q\) the per-egg fledging probability. The immigration rate \(\omega\) is constant, so it contributes nothing to variation in \(\lambda\) by construction — see Section 8.2.

Observation 1 · counts (relative index):

\[ \begin{aligned} \log \mu_i &= \beta_0 + \log N_{t(i)} + \text{week}_{w(i)} + b_e E^{(1)}_i + b_d E^{(2)}_i + u_{k(i)} + \delta_i \\[2pt] \text{count}_i &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_i) \\[2pt] u_k &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{site}}) &&\text{wetland random effect} \\[2pt] \delta_i &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{od}}) &&\text{overdispersion} \end{aligned} \]

\(\beta_0\) is deliberately non-identifiable against the level of \(N\). Expect poor convergence for it, and read abundance as shape rather than magnitude.

Observation 2 · mark–resight (CJS with latent alive-state \(z\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{logit} \phi_{j,t} &= \ell_\phi\!\left[\mathrm{lookup}(t)\right] + \beta^{\text{sex}}_{\mathrm{sex}(j)} + \beta^{\text{tag}}_{\mathrm{tag}(j)} \\[2pt] \operatorname{logit} p_j &= p_0 + \beta^{p}_{\mathrm{tag}(j)} \\[2pt] z_{j,t} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(\phi_{j,t-1}\, z_{j,t-1}\right), \qquad z_{j,\,f(j)} = 1 \\[2pt] y_{j,t} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(p_j\, z_{j,t}\right) \end{aligned} \]

\[ \ell_\phi[1{:}T-1] = \operatorname{logit}\phi_t, \qquad \ell_\phi[T] = \operatorname{logit}\phi_{\text{pre}}, \qquad \ell_\phi[T+1] = \operatorname{logit}\phi_{\text{post}} \]

The two overflow slots absorb the mark–resight intervals that fall outside the count series, rather than discarding those birds.

Observation 3 · productivity (two-part):

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{succ}_m &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(s_{t(m)}\right) &&\text{did the nest fledge anything?} \\[2pt] \text{chicks}_m &\sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(C,\ q \cdot \text{succ}_m\right) &&\text{how many of the clutch} \end{aligned} \]

A single Poisson was rejected here: the brood-size data are bimodal, with nests fledging zero, two, three or four chicks but never exactly one.

Priors.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mu_\phi,\ \mu_s,\ p_0,\ \beta^{\text{sex}},\ \beta^{\text{tag}},\ \beta^{p} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ 1.5) \\[2pt] \beta_0,\ b_e,\ b_d,\ \text{week}_w &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ 5) \\[2pt] \sigma_\phi &\sim \mathrm{Exponential}(2) \\[2pt] \sigma_s,\ \sigma_{\text{site}},\ \sigma_{\text{od}},\ \omega &\sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1) \\[2pt] \phi_{\text{pre}},\ \phi_{\text{post}},\ q &\sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,\ 1) \\[2pt] \pi &\sim \mathrm{Beta}(1.8410,\ 32.5058) &&\text{modern-era recruitment} \\[2pt] \kappa &\sim \mathrm{Beta}(7.6338,\ 8.6569) &&\text{age-1 fraction, both eras} \end{aligned} \]

\(\pi\) and \(\kappa\) are the only informative priors. Both come from scripts/LEYE_recruitment_two_era.R and are passed to the model as constants, so the vague-prior sensitivity run in Section 9.3 is a configuration change rather than a second copy of the model.

The population is declining at roughly 7.0% per year. Adult survival is the best-determined rate in the model. Local recruitment is low, and a substantial share of annual gains is attributable to immigration — but see Recruitment versus immigration for why that split remains uncertain.

phi_ad is the baseline rate for untagged females — the reference level, and the rate that drives the population process model, since the population is overwhelmingly untagged.

5.1 Covariate effects

Effects are shown as odds ratios against the reference levels (female, untagged). An odds ratio below 1 means lower survival — or lower resighting probability — than the reference.

Show code 
orq <- function(col, label, panel) {
  x <- exp(mat[, col])
  data.frame(
    term = label, panel = panel,
    med = median(x),
    lwr = quantile(x, .025, names = FALSE),
    upr = quantile(x, .975, names = FALSE),
    pneg = mean(mat[, col] < 0)
  )
}
fo <- rbind(
  orq("bSex_phi[2]", "Male (vs female)", "Adult survival"),
  orq("bSex_phi[3]", "Unknown sex (vs female)", "Adult survival"),
  orq("bTag_phi[2]", "Geolocator (vs untagged)", "Adult survival"),
  orq("bTag_phi[3]", "GPS (vs untagged)", "Adult survival"),
  orq("bTag_p[2]", "Geolocator (vs untagged)", "Resighting"),
  orq("bTag_p[3]", "GPS (vs untagged)", "Resighting")
)
fo$term <- factor(fo$term, levels = rev(unique(fo$term)))

ggplot(fo, aes(med, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), colour = COL_AD, linewidth = .7) +
  geom_point(colour = COL_AD, size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(aes(x = upr, label = sprintf("P(<1)=%.2f", pneg)),
    hjust = -0.15, size = 2.9, colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(.05, .28))) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Covariate effects (odds-ratio scale)",
    subtitle = "Reference levels: female, untagged",
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_leye() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92"))

6 Recruitment and immigration

6.1 Local recruitment

psi1 and psi2 are the probabilities that a fledged chick survives and returns to breed locally, at age 1 and age 2 respectively. Their priors come from a separate two-era analysis of banded chick cohorts (scripts/LEYE_recruitment_two_era.R, which supersedes the 1990s-only LEYE_juv90_module.R) and are informative but free to update. The level is taken from the modern era; the age-1 versus age-2 split is estimated across both.

Show code 
grid_x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 512)
dens <- function(nm, a, b, lab) {
  po <- density(mat[, nm], from = 0, to = 1)
  rbind(
    data.frame(x = grid_x, y = dbeta(grid_x, a, b), which = "Prior", par = lab),
    data.frame(x = po$x, y = po$y, which = "Posterior", par = lab)
  )
}
dd <- rbind(
  dens("pi_rec", PRIOR_PI["a"], PRIOR_PI["b"], "pi_rec (total recruitment)"),
  dens("kappa", PRIOR_KAPPA["a"], PRIOR_KAPPA["b"], "kappa (fraction at age 1)")
)

ggplot(dd, aes(x, y, colour = which, fill = which)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity", alpha = .18, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~par, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Prior = "grey55", Posterior = COL_REC), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Prior = "grey55", Posterior = COL_REC), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Prior versus posterior", x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_leye() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.y = element_blank())

# How far each posterior actually moved, in units of its own prior. Quoted
# inline below rather than described in words: this callout previously claimed
# `pi_rec` "moves appreciably from its prior", which was never checked against
# the fit and is not true of any fit in this repository.
#   shift  -- change in mean, expressed in prior SDs
#   narrow -- 1 - sd(posterior)/sd(prior), the share of prior spread the data removed
# unname() first: PRIOR_PI["a"] carries the name "a", and c(m = <named>) builds
# "m.a" rather than "m", so p[["m"]] below would fail.
bmom <- function(a, b) {
  a <- unname(a)
  b <- unname(b)
  c(m = a / (a + b), s = sqrt(a * b / ((a + b)^2 * (a + b + 1))))
}
movement <- function(nm, a, b) {
  p <- bmom(a, b)
  x <- mat[, nm]
  list(shift = (mean(x) - p[["m"]]) / p[["s"]], narrow = 1 - sd(x) / p[["s"]])
}
MOVE <- list(
  pi = movement("pi_rec", PRIOR_PI["a"], PRIOR_PI["b"]),
  kap = movement("kappa", PRIOR_KAPPA["a"], PRIOR_KAPPA["b"])
)

The counts carry almost no information about recruitment, and none about its timing. Both posteriors sit essentially on top of their priors. pi_rec moves -0.07 prior standard deviations and the data remove about 10% of its prior spread — a little information about the recruitment level, but not much. kappa moves -0.02 prior SDs and its interval is unchanged to the nearest percent: the age-1 versus age-2 split is exactly what the chick analysis put in.

So the recruitment estimates in Table 3 should be read as the chick histories’ answer, lightly updated, not as something the count data established. That matters because those histories are thin — 18 returning birds across two eras, of which the 1997 cohort alone supplies seven (see Caveats) — and because recruitment and immigration enter λ additively, so what the counts cannot separate is absorbed by omega.

6.2 Has recruitment changed between eras?

The two chick-banding eras are thirty years apart, so the module that supplies the recruitment prior can also be asked whether local recruitment has declined. This is a candidate result, not a settled one, and the figure is built to show why.

Do not report this as an established decline. The direction is well supported and the magnitude is not: the ratio spans a thirteen-fold drop to a modest increase. The comparison rests on 13 and 5 returning birds, and the 1997 cohort — 7 of 11 chicks — supplies most of the 1990s signal on its own. Note also that the left panel is the typical cohort in each era, not the cohort average; see Section 9.3.1.

6.3 Recruitment versus immigration

Show code 
gains <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    year = ipm_years[3:T], source = "Local recruits",
    value = colMeans(mat[, paste0("N_rec[", 3:T, "]")])
  ),
  data.frame(
    year = ipm_years[3:T], source = "Immigrants",
    value = colMeans(mat[, paste0("Imm[", 3:T, "]")])
  )
)

ggplot(gains, aes(year, value, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Local recruits" = COL_REC, "Immigrants" = COL_IMM), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = ipm_years[3:T]) +
  labs(
    title = "Sources of annual gains",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Local recruitment accounts for %.0f%% of gains (95%% CrI %.0f–%.0f%%)",
      100 * mean(share), 100 * quantile(share, .025), 100 * quantile(share, .975)
    ),
    x = NULL, y = "# Birds added"
  ) +
  theme_leye()

This split is uncertain. Recruitment and immigration both add birds, and a relative-scale count index cannot fully separate them. The credible interval on the recruitment share spans 2% to 92%. Informative priors on recruitment narrow this but do not resolve it. Treat the point estimate as indicative, not as a finding.

7 Productivity

Chicks per nest are modeled in two parts: whether the nest succeeded at all, and how many of a four-egg clutch fledged given that it did.

Nest success averages 0.70 (95% CrI 0.59–0.81) and, given success, each egg fledges with probability 0.89 (0.84–0.93). Mean chicks per nest is the product of the two with clutch size, so f_rate keeps the same meaning it had under the earlier single-distribution model and the recruitment equation is unchanged.

This was initially modeled using a single Poisson draw for chicks per nest, but failed the posterior predictive check (see Section 9.2). The observed counts are bimodal — 0, 2, 3 or 4 chicks, with no nest producing exactly one — because a four-egg-clutch shorebird usually either loses the nest entirely or fledges a near-full brood. A Poisson cannot generate that shape at any mean; at the observed mean it expects roughly 16 single-chick nests. The two-part model reproduces the observed frequencies closely.

This also tightened productivity in years with few monitored nests, where the old model fitted a free annual mean to as few as two or three nests. The two-part version borrows strength through the shared clutch size and fledging rate.

Show code 
fr <- as.data.frame(qq("f_rate", 1:(T + 1)))
fr$year <- c(ipm_years, max(ipm_years) + 1)
fr$in_model <- c(rep(TRUE, T), FALSE)

ggplot(fr, aes(year, med)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), colour = "grey55", linewidth = .7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = in_model), size = 2.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(`TRUE` = COL_AD, `FALSE` = "grey60"),
    labels = c(`TRUE` = "In process model", `FALSE` = "Beyond count series"), name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = fr$year) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,4)) +
  labs(title = "Productivity", x = NULL, y = "Chicks per pair") +
  theme_leye() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

8 What drives population change

A transient LTRE (tLTRE), following Koons et al. (2016, 2017). Two questions that sound similar and have different answers:

  • Level — what sustains the population? Mean λ splits across survival, recruitment and immigration.
  • Variance — what drives year-to-year variation in λ?

Everything below is computed per posterior draw, so each contribution carries a credible interval rather than being a point estimate at posterior means.

8.1 What sustains the population

Show code 
lev <- as.data.frame(tl_level)
lev$pathway <- factor(rownames(tl_level), levels = rev(rownames(tl_level)))
# The ARITHMETIC mean lambda, necessarily: this decomposition is additive and
# only the arithmetic mean preserves the identity across years, so the shares
# sum to 100%. It is a larger number than the geometric mean reported as the
# growth rate at the top -- see the note under this figure.
#
# It also covers FEWER transitions: the decomposition needs the previous year's
# productivity, so it starts at s = 2. Both differences are spelled out in the
# note, so compute each one here rather than letting the reader guess which
# accounts for the gap.
lam_mean <- attr(tl_level, "lambda")[["mean"]]
lam_ari_S <- mean(rowMeans(lamt[, tl$S, drop = FALSE]))
lam_geo_S <- mean(exp(rowMeans(log(lamt[, tl$S, drop = FALSE]))))
stopifnot(all.equal(lam_mean, lam_ari_S), ncol(lamt) > length(tl$S))

ggplot(lev, aes(contribution, pathway)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr), colour = COL_AD, linewidth = .7) +
  geom_point(colour = COL_AD, size = 2.6) +
  # label at the interval's right edge, not the point, or it lands on the bar
  geom_text(aes(x = upr, label = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_of_lambda)),
    hjust = -0.25, size = 3.1, colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(.05, .18))) +
  labs(
    title = "Contributions to mean annual λ",
    subtitle = sprintf("Percentages are share of mean annual λ = %.3f", lam_mean),
    x = "Contribution to λ", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_leye()

Survival is the dominant pathway. Recruitment and immigration contribute comparable, smaller amounts — but see the caveat on separating them below.

Two averages of λ appear in this report, and they differ for two reasons. This figure’s denominator is 0.936; the growth rate at the top of the report is 0.930.

Different window. The decomposition needs the previous year’s productivity, so it covers 11 of the 12 transitions, starting at 2015–2016. The dropped first transition is the highest in the series, which is why this figure’s λ sits below the whole-series arithmetic mean of 0.953.

Different average. This figure must average arithmetically, because λs = survival + recruitment + immigration holds exactly in each year and only the arithmetic mean preserves that identity — under any other average the pathway shares would not sum to 100%. The headline is the geometric mean, the correct summary of multiplicative growth: within each posterior draw it equals (N2026/N2014)1/12 exactly. On this figure’s 11 transitions the two averages are 0.936 and 0.916, so about 0.019 of the gap is the averaging alone.

Why averaging growth rates overstates growth. Growth rates multiply rather than add. A population that gains 20% one year and loses 20% the next has λ = 1.2 and λ = 0.8, which average to exactly 1.0 — yet it ends at 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 of where it started, a true rate of \(\sqrt{0.96} = 0.98\) a year. The arithmetic mean of a set of ratios is never below their geometric mean, and the gap widens as the values scatter: to second order it is about σ²/2 on the log scale, which on these 11 transitions comes to 0.023 against the 0.019 actually observed — the right size, the approximation being exact only in the lognormal limit. This is Jensen’s inequality: when a quantity is put through a curved transformation — here a logarithm — averaging before and averaging after give different answers, and the direction is fixed by which way the curve bends.

The difference compounds. Over twelve years the whole-series arithmetic figure implies a 44% decline and the geometric one 58%; the model’s own Ntot path gives the latter. Use the geometric mean for growth, the arithmetic mean only as this decomposition’s denominator.

8.2 What drives year-to-year variation

Most variation in λ is demographic stochasticity, not environmental variation in vital rates. With roughly 25 birds, Poisson noise in who happens to survive, recruit or arrive is a first-order term. A conventional LTRE reports only the driver contributions and would present a fraction of the variance as though it were the whole story.

The cross term is non-zero because population structure (ρ) depends on realized abundance and so carries the same Poisson noise — the smooth and stochastic parts of λ are not independent.

Show code 
ct <- as.data.frame(tl_var$contributions)
ct$driver <- rownames(tl_var$contributions)
ct$label <- driver_labs[ct$driver]
ct$structural_zero <- ct$mean == 0 & ct$lwr == 0 & ct$upr == 0
ct$label <- factor(ct$label, levels = rev(ct$label))

ggplot(ct, aes(mean, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lwr, xmax = upr, colour = structural_zero), linewidth = .7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = structural_zero), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = COL_AD, `TRUE` = "grey65"), guide = "none"
  ) +
  # phi's upper bound sits past the default break, so widen or it gets clipped
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(.04, .08))) +
  labs(
    title = "Contributions to driver-explained variance",
    subtitle = sprintf(
      "Drivers explain %.0f%% of Var(λ); the rest is demographic noise",
      tl_var$partition_pct["driver_explained", "mean"]
    ),
    x = "Contribution to Var(λ)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_leye() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey93"))

Immigration (ω), Recruitment at age 1 (ψ1), Recruitment at age 2 (ψ2) contribute exactly zero — they are single parameters with no year index, so they cannot vary between years by construction, not by evidence. A time-varying immigration rate was fitted and rejected: it absorbed Poisson noise rather than detecting signal (see the README). Separating recruitment from immigration needs data that distinguishes chick-origin returns from newly arrived unbanded adults.

9 Model checking

9.1 Convergence

logB0 is expected to converge poorly. It is the count-model intercept, which is non-identifiable against the absolute level of the population — only their sum enters the linear predictor. This is structural and does not affect \(\lambda\) or any rate reported above.

9.2 Goodness of fit

An IPM can fit one data source well and another badly, and a single pooled statistic would hide that. Each stream is therefore checked separately, using a Freeman–Tukey discrepancy between the observed data and replicates drawn from the fitted model. The Bayesian p-value is P(replicated > observed); values near 0.5 indicate the model reproduces that stream, values near 0 or 1 indicate misfit.

This check earned its keep. The productivity component originally used a single Poisson and returned p = 0.000 — decisive misfit — which led to the two-part nest-success × brood-size model now in use.

Worth noting for anyone repeating this: the productivity data have variance/mean = 1.18, so a routine overdispersion check would have passed them. The misfit was in shape, not variance, and only a discrepancy measure sensitive to the whole distribution detected it.

9.3 Prior sensitivity

Recruitment carries an informative prior from the two-era chick analysis, so the obvious question is whether the result is data-driven or prior-driven. Three companion fits probe it from different directions, each changing only the recruitment hyperparameters:

  • Cohort-averaged — pi_rec centred on the mean across modern cohorts rather than on the typical cohort. See Section 9.3.1 for why these differ.
  • 1997 excluded — pi_rec and kappa re-derived from the two-era fit with the 1997 cohort dropped (Section 6.2). This is the only setting that makes the prior tighter rather than merely moving it: the others shift the mean and leave the width alone, so this one asks whether a harder-pinned pi_rec changes the recruitment/immigration split.
  • Vague — flat Beta(1, 1) on both recruitment parameters, which asks what the counts alone would say.

9.3.1 Which π does the model want?

The recruitment module fits a cohort-level random effect on the logit scale:

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\pi_c) = \mu_\pi + b_{\text{era}}\,\mathbb{1}[\text{modern}_c] + \varepsilon_c, \qquad \varepsilon_c \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_\pi) \]

and reports \(\pi_M = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\mu_\pi + b_{\text{era}})\) — the typical modern cohort, with its random effect set to zero. That is the default prior above.

But the IPM uses \(\pi\) in \(R_t = N\,(f/2)\,\psi\), an expected count, and has no cohort random effect of its own. The constant that reproduces the right expected number of recruits across years is \(\mathrm{E}[\pi_c]\), the mean across cohorts. With \(\sigma_\pi \approx 1.39\) the two differ by about a third — 0.054 against 0.072 — because the random effect is symmetric in logit space, not in probability space.

This is the same curved-transformation effect as in the λ note in Section 8.1, and the same name attaches to it. \(\varepsilon_c\) is symmetric about zero on the logit scale, but \(\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\) bends, so the cohorts above the typical one are pushed further from it in probability than the cohorts below. Back-transforming the typical cohort therefore gives a smaller number than averaging the back-transformed cohorts. The bending is what matters, not the direction of the era effect: the same thing would happen with \(\sigma_\pi\) unchanged and \(b_{\text{era}}\) reversed.

Neither is obviously wrong, so both are reported. Hold the cohort-averaged column loosely for one reason: \(\sigma_\pi\) is estimated from 13 cohorts and 18 returning birds, and the 1997 cohort alone sits at \(\pi_c = 0.58\) against 0.03–0.18 everywhere else. Since \(\sigma_\pi\) is shared across eras, that single cohort inflates the gap for the modern cohorts too.

The count data and the chick data disagree about recruitment.

Under a flat prior the counts pull pi_rec to roughly twice the value the typical-cohort prior supports, and about 1.5 times the cohort-averaged one. The informative priors win because they are the tighter of the two, so the reported recruitment rate reflects the chick data more than the counts.

This is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing over, and three readings are possible without the analysis being able to separate them. The counts cannot distinguish recruitment from immigration, so recruitment inferred from counts absorbs any unmodeled inflow. The assumption that modern chick detection matches the 1990s may be too generous, which would bias recruitment downward. Or local recruitment genuinely is low and immigration genuinely is high.

The recruitment timing is a separate matter and remains almost entirely prior-driven: kappa keeps its central value while its interval widens dramatically under a flat prior.

What survives all three settings. λ is identical to three decimals — the growth rate and everything built on it are unaffected by this choice. What moves is the attribution: as pi_rec rises, omega falls to compensate, tracing the recruitment–immigration ridge. Immigration still outweighs local recruitment under both informative priors, but the margin narrows from 2.2:1 to 1.4:1, and the posterior probability from 0.77 to 0.62. Report the ordering at the conservative end.

10 Caveats

ImportantRead before citing any number above

One 1990s cohort carries most of the recruitment signal. Recruitment priors derive from scripts/LEYE_recruitment_two_era.R, fitted to 122 chicks banded 1995–1999 and 133 banded 2018–2025. Cohort denominators are the real banding totals, recovered from the original records on 2026-09-29; until then 1997 and 1998 were simulated and 1999 was missing, and refitting on the real numbers left every conclusion in this report unchanged.

What the real totals expose is a concentration: the 1997 cohort is 11 chicks with 7 returning, a 64% local return rate against 11%, 7%, 0% and 0% in the other 1990s cohorts and 4% in the modern era. 1997 was a genuinely low-effort season — 21 adults marked, against 52/48/36/21 in the surrounding years — so the small denominator is real rather than an artefact. But recruitment probability scales inversely with these denominators, so psi from the 1990s rests heavily on that one cohort.

Recruitment and immigration are confounded, as described above.

Abundance is relative. Do not report absolute population size.

psi is not survival. It is survival combined with returning to breed locally. Birds that survive but settle elsewhere are excluded; immigration is modeled separately through omega.

Counts end in 2025 while survival and productivity run to 2026. The extra survival interval and productivity year are estimated in dedicated pooled parameters rather than being discarded, and do not drive the trajectory.

```{r}
#| label: load
#| include: false

# Run from the project root regardless of where the .qmd lives.
proj <- normalizePath(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)), ".."))
setwd(proj)

# Rebuild the data context (ipm_years, T, cjs_int_start, cjs, dp ...) exactly as
# the model saw it. SKIP_RUN keeps this to object definitions -- no refitting.
SKIP_RUN <- TRUE
source("scripts/LEYE_IPM.R")

# Locate the cached posterior.
#
# Use the CANONICAL filename, not a newest-match glob. A glob on
# LEYE_IPM_samples*.rds also matches companion and archive fits
# (vague-priors, time-varying-omega, dated caches), and picking whichever is
# newest silently builds the report from whichever model was last refitted.
# That fails loudly only if the parameter names happen to differ; if they
# match, the report renders cleanly from the wrong posterior.
CANONICAL <- "LEYE_IPM_samples.rds"
samples_path <- params$samples_path
if (is.null(samples_path)) {
  if (!file.exists(CANONICAL)) {
    stop(
      "No cached posterior at '", CANONICAL, "'. Fit the model first ",
      "(scripts/LEYE_IPM.R or scripts/LEYE_IPM_run_parallel.R), or pass ",
      "-P samples_path:<file>."
    )
  }
  samples_path <- CANONICAL
}

# The parallel wrapper's lapply() strips the mcmc.list class, and as.matrix()
# on the resulting plain list silently returns a 3x1 matrix instead of erroring.
# Re-wrap defensively so the report cannot be built on garbage.
samples <- readRDS(samples_path)

# Provenance guard. A cache fitted under a different model version renders
# perfectly well and simply shows the wrong numbers, so refuse rather than warn.
cache_status <- ipm_cache_status(samples)
if (cache_status == "stale") {
  stop(
    "'", samples_path, "' was fitted under a DIFFERENT version of the model ",
    "than the one in scripts/LEYE_IPM.R. Refit before rendering, or the report ",
    "will present the previous fit's results as current. (Comments and ",
    "formatting are excluded from the fingerprint, so this reflects a real ",
    "change to structure, constants, priors or data.)"
  )
}

# as.mcmc.list() drops attributes, so read provenance before converting. The
# parallel wrapper's lapply() used to strip the mcmc.list class, and as.matrix()
# on a plain list silently returns a 3 x 1 matrix -- re-wrap defensively.
fit_priors <- attr(samples, "ipm_provenance")$priors
if (!inherits(samples, "mcmc.list")) samples <- coda::as.mcmc.list(samples)
mat <- as.matrix(samples)

n_chains <- coda::nchain(samples)
n_draws <- nrow(mat)
stopifnot(n_draws > 100) # guard against the silent-truncation failure above

# Recruitment priors, taken from the fit's own provenance stamp and falling back
# to the constants in scripts/LEYE_IPM.R. These were hard-coded literals until
# 2026-10-02 and had gone stale: they still held the 1990s-only Beta(2.268,
# 13.610) and Beta(6.054, 6.309) long after the model moved to the two-era fits,
# so the prior-vs-posterior comparison was drawn against a prior the model never
# used. Read them, never retype them.
prior_of <- function(a, b) {
  if (!is.null(fit_priors)) {
    c(a = fit_priors[[a]], b = fit_priors[[b]])
  } else {
    c(a = constants[[a]], b = constants[[b]])
  }
}
PRIOR_PI <- prior_of("a_pi", "b_pi")
PRIOR_KAPPA <- prior_of("a_kap", "b_kap")

# omega is a scalar in some fits and a year-indexed vector in others. Resolve
# once here so the rest of the report does not care which it is.
omega_tv <- any(grepl("^omega\\[", colnames(mat)))
omega_draws <- if (omega_tv) mat[, "omega_bar"] else mat[, "omega"]

# tLTRE. Computed here from the SAME posterior loaded above rather than read
# from LEYE_tLTRE_results.rds, so the decomposition cannot silently belong to a
# different fit than the numbers everywhere else in this report. Sourcing with
# SKIP_TLTRE_RUN loads the functions without running the script's own report.
SKIP_TLTRE_RUN <- TRUE
source("scripts/LEYE_tLTRE.R")
tl <- tltre_series(mat, T)
tltre_check(tl) # stops the render if the exact identity ever breaks
tl_level <- tltre_level(tl)
tl_var <- tltre_variance(tl)

driver_labs <- c(
  phi = "Adult survival (φ)",
  omega = "Immigration (ω)",
  f_t = "Productivity, year t",
  f_lag = "Productivity, year t−1",
  rho = "Population structure (ρ)",
  psi1 = "Recruitment at age 1 (ψ1)",
  psi2 = "Recruitment at age 2 (ψ2)"
)
# NB: plain "ψ1" not "ψ₁" -- the Unicode subscript has no glyph in the default
# plotting font and renders as a tofu box on the axis.

q <- function(x) {
  c(
    mean = mean(x),
    med = median(x),
    lwr = quantile(x, .025, names = FALSE),
    upr = quantile(x, .975, names = FALSE)
  )
}
qq <- function(stem, idx) {
  t(vapply(paste0(stem, "[", idx, "]"), function(cn) q(mat[, cn]), numeric(4)))
}

# House table style: one call so every table in the report matches.
tbl <- function(x, title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, dec = 3) {
  g <- gt(x)
  if (!is.null(title)) g <- tab_header(g, title = title, subtitle = subtitle)
  g |>
    fmt_number(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = dec) |>
    opt_row_striping() |>
    tab_options(
      table.font.size = px(13),
      heading.title.font.size = px(15),
      heading.subtitle.font.size = px(12),
      column_labels.font.weight = "600",
      data_row.padding = px(4),
      table.border.top.style = "none"
    )
}

# Shared plot look.
theme_leye <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),

      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey45", hjust = 0, size = 9),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = "grey25")
    )
}

COL_REC <- "#2e8b57"
COL_IMM <- "#c0504d"

trans_yr <- ipm_years[-T]
trans_lab <- paste0(trans_yr, "–", trans_yr + 1)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## How to read this report

Abundance is estimated on a **relative** scale — the counts are a volunteer index,
not a census. Read the *shape* of the trajectory and the growth rate $\lambda$;
the absolute number of birds is not identified and is not reported here.

Recruitment (`psi1`, `psi2`) is a **composite** probability: survive **and**
return to breed locally. It is not juvenile survival, and should not be compared
against published juvenile survival estimates.
:::

# Overview

This integrated population model combines three data sources into one likelihood
so that each informs a shared set of demographic rates.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| echo: false

data.frame(
  Source = c("Abundance", "Survival", "Productivity"),
  Data = c(
    "Volunteer wetland counts",
    "Adult mark–resight (CJS)",
    "Nest productivity"
  ),
  # Derived, never typed: hard-coded ranges here went stale the moment the
  # count series was extended to 2026.
  Years = vapply(
    list(count_years, cjs_years, prod_years),
    function(y) sprintf("%d–%d", min(y), max(y)), character(1)
  ),
  Detail = c(
    sprintf("%d records, %d wetlands, 3 weekly visits", nCount, nWet),
    sprintf("%d individuals, sex + tag-type covariates", cjs$nind),
    sprintf("%d nests, chicks per nest", nProd)
  )
) |>
  tbl("Data sources") |>
  cols_align("left")
```

![Study area. **A** The Anchorage bowl, with the 27 wetlands in the IPM's count stream; the mark–resight and nest monitoring also sit here. The five distant wetlands in the volunteer survey are surveyed but not fitted, and are not shown (see below). Bubble area is the mean number of Lesser Yellowlegs per survey — a raw count, not an abundance estimate, and uncorrected for detection, effort or wetland area. Hollow circles are wetlands that have never produced a detection. Site coordinates are in `manuscript/figures/study_area_sites.csv`. **B** Location in Alaska. Shoreline from GSHHG full resolution (Wessel & Smith 1996).](../manuscript/figures/study_area_bowl.png){#fig-studyarea}

::: {.callout-note}
## The counts cover the same ground as the demographic data — deliberately

The volunteer survey covers 32 wetlands across roughly 67 km of upper Cook Inlet,
but every marked bird and every monitored nest comes from the Anchorage bowl
(@fig-studyarea). Fitting all 32 would make λ a statement about a
wider population than the survival and productivity estimates meant to explain it, and
the decomposition further down this report would be comparing the two. Since
2026-11-04 the count stream is restricted to the 27 wetlands in the bowl, dropping both
Palmer Hay Flats accesses, Eklutna, Big Lake and Lynn Fuller's Ponds — 37–67 km out,
and 22.6% of all birds counted. They are not drawn in @fig-studyarea.

**The restriction makes the decline steeper, not weaker:** λ 0.939 → 0.930, with
P(λ < 1) = 0.997 either way. The wider-area fit is kept as a sensitivity. The list and
reasoning are at the top of `scripts/LEYE_IPM.R`.
:::

Recruitment carries a **two-year lag**: chicks are absent from the breeding site
until they recruit, and chick data from both eras show recruitment split roughly
evenly between ages 1 and 2. Recruits enter the breeding class directly, so there
is no separate juvenile stage — volunteer counts cannot distinguish non-breeding
age-1 birds from breeding adults. The full formulation follows.

# Model structure

## Life cycle and data sources

![Life cycle of the modeled population. Boxes are states, arrows are the demographic rates that move birds between them, and the colours identify which data source informs each rate. `psi1` and `psi2` are composite survive-and-return-locally probabilities, not annual survival: a bird that survives but settles elsewhere is not a local recruit.](../manuscript/figures/life_cycle.svg){#fig-lifecycle}

## Model graph

![Directed graph of the integrated model, in the style of Kéry & Schaub. Shaded nodes are observed data, unshaded nodes are estimated quantities, and the three observation submodels all attach to the same latent series of breeding adults `N`. That shared state is what makes this an integrated model rather than three analyses reported together.](../manuscript/figures/ipm_dag.svg){#fig-dag}

## Statistical formulation

Transcribed from `scripts/LEYE_IPM.R`. Indices: $t$ = year (1…$T$,
`r sprintf("%d–%d", min(ipm_years), max(ipm_years))`),
$i$ = count record, $j$ = marked individual, $m$ = nest, $w$ = survey week,
$k$ = wetland.

**Process model.** Two free initial years, because recruitment lags two years and
there is nothing to build $N_1$ and $N_2$ from:

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_1,\, N_2 &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ 50)\ \text{truncated at } 0 \\[2pt]
R_t &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(N_{t-1}\,\frac{f_{t-1}}{2}\,\psi_1
        \;+\; N_{t-2}\,\frac{f_{t-2}}{2}\,\psi_2\right) \\[2pt]
S_t &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(N_{t-1}\,\phi_{t-1}\right) \\[2pt]
I_t &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(N_{t-1}\,\omega\right) \\[2pt]
N_t &= S_t + R_t + I_t \\[2pt]
\lambda_t &= N_{t+1} \,/\, N_t
\end{aligned}
\qquad t = 3,\dots,T
$$

**Vital rates.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit} \phi_t &= \mu_\phi + \varepsilon_{\phi,t},
  &\varepsilon_{\phi,t} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_\phi)
  &&\text{adult survival} \\[2pt]
\operatorname{logit} s_t &= \mu_s + \varepsilon_{s,t},
  &\varepsilon_{s,t} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_s)
  &&\text{nest success} \\[2pt]
f_t &= s_t \cdot C \cdot q &&&&\text{fledglings per pair} \\[2pt]
\psi_1 &= \pi\,\kappa &&&&\text{recruit at age 1} \\[2pt]
\psi_2 &= \pi\,(1-\kappa) &&&&\text{recruit at age 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $C = 4$ (modal clutch) and $q$ the per-egg fledging probability. The
immigration rate $\omega$ is constant, so it contributes nothing to *variation*
in $\lambda$ by construction — see @sec-variance.

**Observation 1 · counts** (relative index):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log \mu_i &= \beta_0 + \log N_{t(i)} + \text{week}_{w(i)}
   + b_e E^{(1)}_i + b_d E^{(2)}_i + u_{k(i)} + \delta_i \\[2pt]
\text{count}_i &\sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_i) \\[2pt]
u_k &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{site}})
   &&\text{wetland random effect} \\[2pt]
\delta_i &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ \sigma_{\text{od}})
   &&\text{overdispersion}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\beta_0$ is deliberately non-identifiable against the level of $N$. Expect poor
convergence for it, and read abundance as shape rather than magnitude.

**Observation 2 · mark–resight** (CJS with latent alive-state $z$):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit} \phi_{j,t} &= \ell_\phi\!\left[\mathrm{lookup}(t)\right]
   + \beta^{\text{sex}}_{\mathrm{sex}(j)} + \beta^{\text{tag}}_{\mathrm{tag}(j)} \\[2pt]
\operatorname{logit} p_j &= p_0 + \beta^{p}_{\mathrm{tag}(j)} \\[2pt]
z_{j,t} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(\phi_{j,t-1}\, z_{j,t-1}\right),
   \qquad z_{j,\,f(j)} = 1 \\[2pt]
y_{j,t} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(p_j\, z_{j,t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\ell_\phi[1{:}T-1] = \operatorname{logit}\phi_t, \qquad
\ell_\phi[T] = \operatorname{logit}\phi_{\text{pre}}, \qquad
\ell_\phi[T+1] = \operatorname{logit}\phi_{\text{post}}
$$

The two overflow slots absorb the mark–resight intervals that fall outside the
count series, rather than discarding those birds.

**Observation 3 · productivity** (two-part):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{succ}_m &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(s_{t(m)}\right)
   &&\text{did the nest fledge anything?} \\[2pt]
\text{chicks}_m &\sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(C,\ q \cdot \text{succ}_m\right)
   &&\text{how many of the clutch}
\end{aligned}
$$

A single Poisson was rejected here: the brood-size data are bimodal, with nests
fledging zero, two, three or four chicks but never exactly one.

**Priors.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_\phi,\ \mu_s,\ p_0,\ \beta^{\text{sex}},\ \beta^{\text{tag}},\ \beta^{p}
   &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ 1.5) \\[2pt]
\beta_0,\ b_e,\ b_d,\ \text{week}_w &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\ 5) \\[2pt]
\sigma_\phi &\sim \mathrm{Exponential}(2) \\[2pt]
\sigma_s,\ \sigma_{\text{site}},\ \sigma_{\text{od}},\ \omega
   &\sim \mathrm{Exponential}(1) \\[2pt]
\phi_{\text{pre}},\ \phi_{\text{post}},\ q &\sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,\ 1) \\[2pt]
\pi &\sim \mathrm{Beta}(1.8410,\ 32.5058)
   &&\text{modern-era recruitment} \\[2pt]
\kappa &\sim \mathrm{Beta}(7.6338,\ 8.6569)
   &&\text{age-1 fraction, both eras}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\pi$ and $\kappa$ are the **only** informative priors. Both come from
`scripts/LEYE_recruitment_two_era.R` and are passed to the model as constants, so
the vague-prior sensitivity run in @sec-prior-sens is a configuration change
rather than a second copy of the model.

# Headline results

```{r}
#| label: headline
#| echo: false

# TWO summaries of lambda, and they are not interchangeable.
#
# `geolam` is the long-run growth rate: the GEOMETRIC mean across years, taken
# within each draw. It is the only summary that reproduces what the population
# actually does -- per draw it equals (N_tot[T]/N_tot[1])^(1/(T-1)) to machine
# precision, because that is an algebraic identity, not an approximation.
#
# `arilam` is the ARITHMETIC mean across years. It is NOT a growth rate; with a
# within-draw sd of log lambda around 0.22 it sits about 0.023 above the
# geometric mean by Jensen's inequality (sigma^2/2 predicts 0.0229 and the
# observed gap is 0.0229), which compounds to a 14-point difference over twelve
# years. It is reported only where an ADDITIVE decomposition
# needs it: lambda[s] = surv_pc[s] + rec_pc[s] + imm_pc[s] is exact, and
# averaging it across years stays exact only for the arithmetic mean, so the
# tLTRE level figure must use `arilam` as its denominator or the pathway shares
# would not sum to 100%. See tltre_level() in scripts/LEYE_tLTRE.R.
#
# This file previously used the arithmetic mean everywhere and LABELLED it a
# geometric mean, which understated the decline. On the count stream in use at
# the time (all 32 wetlands) that was 0.959 with P(lambda<1) = 0.94, against the
# 0.939 and P = 0.997 the model's own N_tot trajectory implied. Both of those
# are full-panel numbers; the current model fits the Anchorage bowl only.
lamt <- mat[, paste0("lambda[", 1:(T - 1), "]")]
lam <- exp(rowMeans(log(lamt)))
geolam <- mean(lam)
geolam_ci <- quantile(lam, c(.025, .975))
arilam <- rowMeans(lamt)
Rm <- rowSums(mat[, paste0("N_rec[", 3:T, "]")])
Im <- rowSums(mat[, paste0("Imm[", 3:T, "]")])
# Recruits and immigrants are Poisson counts, so a draw with no gains at all is
# legitimate and gives 0/0. Rare, but it halts the whole render at quantile():
# the share is undefined for those draws, not zero, so drop them and count them.
gains_tot <- Rm + Im
share <- Rm[gains_tot > 0] / gains_tot[gains_tot > 0]
share_undef <- sum(gains_tot == 0)

card <- function(value, label, sub, colour) {
  sprintf(
    '<div class="kpi" style="border-top-color:%s"><div class="kpi-v">%s</div>
     <div class="kpi-l">%s</div><div class="kpi-s">%s</div></div>',
    colour, value, label, sub
  )
}
htmltools::HTML(paste0(
  '<div class="kpi-row">',
  card(
    sprintf("%.3f", geolam), "Population growth (λ)",
    sprintf("%.3f – %.3f &nbsp;|&nbsp; %.1f%%/yr", geolam_ci[1], geolam_ci[2], 100 * (geolam - 1)),
    "#c0504d"
  ),
  card(
    sprintf("%.2f", mean(mat[, "phi_ad[1]"])), "Adult survival",
    "annual, untagged female baseline", COL_AD
  ),
  card(
    sprintf("%.3f", mean(mat[, "pi_rec"])), "Local recruitment",
    sprintf("ψ₁ %.3f &nbsp; ψ₂ %.3f", mean(mat[, "psi1"]), mean(mat[, "psi2"])),
    COL_REC
  ),
  card(
    sprintf("%.3f", mean(omega_draws)), "Immigration rate (ω)",
    sprintf("%.0f%% of annual gains", 100 * (1 - mean(share))),
    COL_IMM
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

The population is declining at roughly
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", abs(100 * (geolam - 1)))` per year. Adult survival is the
best-determined rate in the model. Local recruitment is low, and a substantial
share of annual gains is attributable to immigration — but see
[Recruitment versus immigration] for why that split remains uncertain.
